utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom. Good morning, Witness C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I shall be cross-examining you now as the Defence counsel for the other accused. My name is Goran Mikulicic. I'm an attorney at law in Zagreb, and I shall put a few questions to you, and I would like you to answer them to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. C, you said during your introductory remarks that you finished the Medresa, a religious school in Sarajevo. Are you a believer, yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you are a practicing believer? Do you go to prayers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness C, how was religion treated in the Territorial Defence of the BH army and later in the BH army itself? The members of the armed forces, did they have an opportunity to practice their religion and express their religious beliefs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this left to the initiative of every individual soldier or was it organised some way in the units of the Territorial Defence or later the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: It was the personal affair of every member of the BH army, and it was up to the units, themselves, to create conditions, at the request of the members of the armed forces, for practising their religion or conducting their religious services, if this is made possible due to the situation in terms of combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Do you remember any cases, Mr. C, when religious officials came to see the units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, Witness C, did any religious officials hold any command positions in the units of the BH army? I'm referring to imams.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: In the unit that I was in, there was not that case, that an imam commanded a unit, I mean from platoon upwards, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Witness C, you said, during your introductory remarks, that on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 8th of April, 1992, a danger of war was officially proclaimed and that the citizens had to report to Territorial Defence staffs until the 15th of April, 1992. Is that a correct figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, then, what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: When the Defence counsel asked me, I just confirmed that on the 20th of June, 1992, the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared, on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a danger of war and general mobilisation. Before that, an enactment was passed by the same organ on the 8th of April, 1992, that there was an immediate threat of war on the territory of the Republic, and all military conscripts, all military-aged men, were requested to report to Territorial Defence staffs by the 15th of April. This was an enactment that was published in the official gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) May I go on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who carried out this mobilisation of military-age population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Until after the 20th of June, to the best of my knowledge, nobody carried out mobilisation because until then it was only volunteers who were reporting to Territorial Defence staffs. On the 25th of May, 1992, the military presidency of the municipality of Novi Travnik also publicly invited all military-age men to report to the Territorial Defence staff in order to be taken into the defence units of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who supervised the exercise of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anybody having done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness C, was mobilisation carried out exclusively in terms of the armed forces or was mobilisation also carried out in other ways? I'm actually referring to civilian defence units or work duty units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in that sense, the situation in Novi Travnik was a very special one. I don't know when the civil defence staff started to operate and when they started manning their own units. I also know that it was only in 1993, in the second half of '93 and the beginning of '94, that certain conditions were created for this kind of an exercise. They started addressing defence secretariats, and various people received work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Witness C, there was also mobilisation in terms of work duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly when. In certain segments such as state organs and certain enterprises, companies, institutions, I don't know who did this when. But, of course, a lot of time has gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, do you know what the criterion was for a military-aged man or woman to be mobilised in the armed forces or into a work duty unit? What was the distinctive criterion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: There was the legal criterion, as you know. A military-age man is a man age 18 to 60, and that was the criterion according to law. And of course it was a question of one's health as well, and this was of decisive importance as to why somebody would receive work duty whereas others would be sent to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that both forms of mobilisation were actually a contribution to the defence of the army of -- in defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say "Yes" to that. At any rate, institutions, state agencies, enterprises, in the situation as it was, contributed to keeping up a normal life in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, you said that a state of war was declared and general mobilisation, too. Against who was a state of war declared? Who was the enemy at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: You should ask the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are the ones who passed this decision. There is a document called the "Platform of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina", and this was published in the official gazette number 7 of 1992, and you can read there what the definition of "aggression" is and what the state of war was, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, and thank you for teaching me, Witness C. But at this point, it is not the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that is testifying before this Court but it is you. I'm asking you whether you know the answer to this. If you do not know the answer, please say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I said that it is the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that passed this decision, and I only observed the decision that was passed by the competent state authority, that is to say, the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witnesses C, it is obvious from your answer that you read this decision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you read in this decision? Who is the enemy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I just wonder if we're going to get very far in this. In due course you can produce the document, I expect, or you call for the document and all then will be made clear. I think arguing with the witness is not going to take us much further. If you would like to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, are you aware of what the work duty units did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Not exactly. This was outside the sphere of my own interests at that period of time. I just know en passant that sometimes work duty units try to clear the terrain and do other things. They worked in schools, they worked in kindergartens, they worked in state agencies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did work duty units also work on building fortifications for the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No. That was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, in your testimony you said that in order to meet the needs of the armed forces of the BH army a code of conduct was passed for the troops. Could you tell us something about this? Who prescribed this code of conduct and in which way did it enter into force, if it entered into force at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: This code entered into force at the beginning of July by the main staff, I think it was called, of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting. Which year is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: 1992, of course. We received, by telegraph, seven or eight sentences that referred to the code of conduct of members of the BH army, how to behave in combat, how to treat civilians, how to treat prisoners, how to behave in respect of international law of war, something like that. I think it was seven or eight sentences altogether, this code. It was really on a small piece of paper, and every member of the army received this little piece of paper at the time, and they were all duty-bound to carry it and to behave in keeping with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Now, let us move on to a different subject, Witness C. In your testimony, on several occasions you used certain words which I would like you to clarify for us. For example, you talked about a "roadblock" and you talked about a "checkpoint." Could you tell us what the distinction is between the two, if any, and what they actually denote?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Checkpoint, on the basis of what I saw as I was passing them myself, I take this to be a point where members of the civilian police or possibly military police check vehicles and persons that pass there and, also, goods if there are any goods in the vehicles concerned. Perhaps it is a question of identification too. So that is what a checkpoint would be. Whereas a roadblock is a barrier. It is not there to check anyone or anything. This is a physical barrier on a road. As a rule, there are armed persons who are standing by that roadblock and prohibiting the passing of vehicles, and persons, and goods too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the main distinction between the two would be the following: A checkpoint is a police checkpoint and a roadblock is a military point? Could we infer that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes. Perhaps that classification would be possible. I am not aware of the police ever having done this, I mean, the civilian police putting up a roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, could you tell us what were the checkpoints of the BH army like by the motel of Ravno Rostovo or, rather, was this a checkpoint or was this a roadblock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I went that way once, and I know it was merely a checkpoint where, at least at the time that I went through it, nobody stopped one. There were some physical impediments, barriers, so that one had to slow down one's vehicle. I think there was a sentry post near these obstacles on the road, and a soldier stood there, who was present at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that that checkpoint was controlled by the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when I went that way, there were members of the BH army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On what road was that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: That checkpoint was exactly at the place, that is, on the regional road. It was Novi Travnik-Bugojno regional road, precisely at the place where the access road joins from Gornji Vakuf, Novi Travnik, from the place Stara Opara, it went through Lukova and there joined the regional road. So at this particular junction was the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Stari Opara. Was there such a point in Opara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Next to the school. There were the police, civilian police there as of summer '92, as far as I know. The Ministry of the Interior or, rather, the public security station of Novi Travnik kept some policemen there and they had a checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Pavlovica next to the mountaineer's cottage, what was the situation there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I did come across a checkpoint there but it must have been as late as '93, and I should say after July '93, when I moved around that area. I could see there was a military police checkpoint but the one in Opara was out of work by that time. They must have simply changed it. So there was no checkpoint in Opara at the time. At that time they were only there and at Nedeljnik next to the surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In town itself next to the fire brigade centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Next to the fire brigade centre there has never been a checkpoint. I only mentioned at some point that on the 18th of June '92, about an hour and a half, there was a roadblock at that entry into the former Mali Raj coffee bar, and there was a small roadblock set up by the members of the Territorial Defence, but they were in existence for not long -- I mean, both of them for not longer than an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And next to the elementary school in the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No, next to the Vodovod. Vodovod is about four kilometres out of Novi Travnik. I don't know. I never went that way so that I never saw a checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: The elementary school is next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, to be quite clear about this, when we talked about all these places, tell us, who controlled all those sites?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Which ones do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I meant a number of sites, Ravno Rostovo, Opara, Pavlovica, fire brigade, Vodovod. Who controlled them? Was it under the control of the BH army or was it under the control of the HVO or perhaps by a third party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Ravno Rostovo was more or less, over a long period of time, was controlled by the BH army. Vodovod was never there any particular control, because the residents of the area have lived for a long time together, until the 4th of July when the Croat population left that area. The fire brigade centre was always on the centre of the BH army line. Opara has always been a village which was in the zone controlled by the armija. As for the Nedeljnik checkpoint, I think I said when it was in operation I think that only as of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Talking about Vodovod, Witness C, do you remember that incident where four HVO officers went missing? Was it next to the Vodovod?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday. It was further away from Vodovod. I denoted in my war logbook, and I remember that I noted that that afternoon the police came across an empty vehicle on the Vodovod-Kovacici road, and that it was assumed that there had been four persons in that vehicle, HVO members, who were not in the vehicle at the time, and it was, I assume, that they had been ill-treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: About those checkpoints and roadblocks, the ones you mentioned, you said they were on regional roads leading to Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No, not Travnik. Not Travnik. Not Travnik. I never said Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry. So my question is: Did the Croats in that area -- could the Croats in that area travel to Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf without being hauled in and having to go through those checkpoints, that is, roadblocks, or did they have to undergo control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: HVO members, that would be more accurate, had the checkpoint on the road to Gornji Vakuf not far from the Nedeljnik checkpoint manned by the civilian police as of July 1993. Before that there was, throughout the previous period of time, there was a checkpoint --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness C, but I'm asking you to answer my questions. Could the Croats, HVO members, pass through those checkpoints controlled by the BH army without being stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout, yes, except during armed conflicts. During armed conflicts, naturally, one could not cross -- one could not go through defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, when you spoke about conflicts which took place in the town of Novi Travnik itself, you mentioned HVO and HOS units. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So my question is: Do you know where the HOS's command was and where the HVO command was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I've repeated it a number of times, and I'll repeat it for the fifth time if need be, where the command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So where was the HOS command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I said that the HOS unit had its command at the new hotel, that is the Novi Travnik Hotel, and the HVO staff was at the old hotel for a long time then in Bratstvo, in Novi Travnik. Then they moved over to Novi Travnik Hotel, I guess, when that unit ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that during clashes in the town of Novi Travnik, HVO took part. Do you know which HVO units were involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I do not remember. I spoke about conflicts in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik there were several conflicts between the armijas and HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, the first conflict, do you know which HVO units participated in the first conflict in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I do not know that, because I was at the workers' centre all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know which HVO units participated in the second conflict in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know which HVO units participated in the third conflict in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I do not know. Apart from the unit, that is HVO brigade Stjepan Tomasevic which operated in our area. I do not know about our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Witness C, in your written statement, you spoke about how Croats left the village of Hadzici -- Hodzici, I'm sorry, in 1993, and you said that, in point of fact, you did not know why the Croats left that day, the 17th of June. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you still affirming that you do not know why the Croats left the villages Hadzici, Rude, Gornji Pec, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know why they left. I do not know why they went to the line which before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, you said you did not know, so I will move on. On two occasions, I believe, you gave statements to the investigator of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I gave my statements twice but that was one statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Witness C, I will now show you what you answered to the investigator when he asked you the same question. It is your statement of the 8th of November, 1997. Page 14, you say that there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Mikulicic. Have you given the witness a copy of the statement? He should have a copy if you're going to read out of it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) (No translation.) Excuse me. I'm trying to find my way about this text, the text in B/C/S/, that is, in the original in the Bosnian language. There is a difference -- there is a lag between pages in the English version and the text in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mikulicic, so we don't waste time, read out the passage that you want to put to the witness and then show it to him so that he can see it and comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I understand. I found it. Mr. Usher, will you please show the witness the part of the text we are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, will you please read aloud the one-but-last paragraph of your statement that you have in your hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: "The fighting between Armija and the HVO in the area of Djakovici was waged around the 12th of June, 1993. In consequence of the offensive, HVO evacuated the population for villages Djakovici, Rude, Pecine, Mravinjac and so on and so forth. When the civilian population left the village of Margetici and when those positions were left by the HVO, the area fell in the hands of the Armija."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the fragment. Is that what you told the Tribunal's investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I signed the statement in English, and I hope this is a correct translation of what I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Will you please then explain to us the difference between what you said today and what you told the Tribunal's investigator? What is correct? You are now saying that you do not know why the Croat population left those villages, and in your written statement which you gave to the investigator, it was that the Croat population left those villages in the aftermath of conflicts and the evacuation carried out by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: But then you have to quote part of my -- of what I said here, and as far as I remember, I said that the civilian population from these villages, together with the HVO, left that area on the 16th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I think we understand it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: And that, to my mind, is the evacuation by the HVO, because the HVO were facing the Chetnik line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Witness C. We understand it all now. Now, I should like to ask Mr. Usher to -- I just asked Mr. Usher to place before the witness the map of the territory of the municipality of Novi Travnik. It is 2662,3. Witness C, will you please use this black marker that you have next to you to draw the boundaries of the Novi Travnik municipality on this map? Needless to say, you don't have to be 100 per cent accurate, but to the best of your recollection. Will you please use the black marker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I apologise in advance. The boundaries that I've drawn now will perhaps deviate from the actual state of affairs, because the scale of this map is such that one cannot be truly precise. But roughly, we start from the road to Travnik, so we're in Nevic Polje, and then to the left down the boundary to the municipality of Slimena, or in front of it, then below Bilenica, then Mravinjac, then beyond Karamija (phoen) towards Bugojno, then in front of Zijamet, roughly this way to Kalin and then Ravno Rostovo. That was the boundary. Just a moment. Towards Gornji Vakuf, and ended up at Peluka (phoen). It could be about here, then more like this, and then including Sebesic, then towards the boundary with Busovaca reaching the boundary with the Vitez municipality, and then across Busic Karavan (phoen), above Bucici, above Balici towards Mosunj, coming down to this boundary here. This would be it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Your Honours, I'm going to ask the witness to mark something on this map, and we'll show that on the ELMO so that it would be obvious to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, please look at the borders of the municipality of Novi Travnik, the ones that you marked, and now look at the separation line between the BH army and the HVO, as it was established after the first -- rather after the second conflict in 1992. Could you mark that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. He has marked on one map already, which is 2612,3(a), he has marked the separation line or the front line. Perhaps the witness could have that so he could see what he marked before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, with all due respect, the witness marked the line of separation vis-à-vis the Serb units, and I'm asking the witness to mark the separation line between the HVO and the BH army respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let him have both maps in front of him, and the latest map had better be 2612,3(b).

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: On the previous map, I marked the HVO units and the BH army units from Novi Travnik only, held a line of defence against a Serb aggressor --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, please listen to me carefully. We're not talking about the Serb aggressor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, look, I have the map in front of me, and the president of this Trial Chamber asked me to look at this map, so now I'm talking about the border of the municipality. And this is the line that was held by the HVO and the BH army vis-à-vis this other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, I'm going to repeat my question, please. On this map, where you just marked the boundaries of the municipality of Novi Travnik, would you please mark the line of separation between the HVO and the BH army respectively?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the second conflict.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: But it's impossible to do that. I already said that the line of separation was established only in the town itself. Elsewhere, there was not a line that was established and that lasted those six or seven days. I did this on the map of town, and I've already done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that, Witness C. Now I would like to ask you something else. Could you please use a red marker to show the part of the Novi Travnik municipality that you've just marked on the map that was under HVO control, and then use the green marker to show the part that was held by the BH army, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: There is also a lack of accuracy in this question, too. There were different periods --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: In 1993, that would mean to make -- it would mean making three maps, at least, of different situations that occurred from the 9th of June, 1993, until October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I don't think we're going to get much further on these maps. The witness has given his answer. He finds it difficult if not impossible to do, so shall we move on to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I see. So I imagine that that is the way this statement is going to be assessed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. C, you mentioned the map of the town of Novi Travnik that you gave the Court. I'm talking about an exhibit, Z1962,B. I would like to ask the usher to show the witness that map, please. So I'm talking about Z1962,B. Mr. C, my question is the following: Why has the western part of the town of Novi Travnik not been marked on this map, or at least not extensively so? Was there any special reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: There was no reason for it. This is simply a drawing that existed in the old headquarters in 1992, so we simply made use of an old paper where there was some kind of a drawing of the town. I didn't have anything else, so I simply wanted to depict what I had spoken about concerning the first conflict and the second conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness C, who lives in the western part of the town of Novi Travnik? What is the population there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in Novi Travnik, there were 23 point something per cent of Croats, 38 per cent Serbs, and there were three Bosniaks less than Serbs, three less, literally. So I presented this ethnic composition of the population, and I don't know whether they were evenly distributed or not throughout town, but practically they did live in all parts of town. As the previous Defence counsel said, it was a small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in this part of town, are there many houses there, buildings, or according to this map, is it an empty part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: If you look at this map and if you see the north, and if you say that there is no town on the western side, I'm telling you that there is the street of Kalinska, rather the street of the 4th of July, and Omladinska Street. Then above Omladinska Street is the village of Isakovici. And then there is the village of Kasapovici after the street of the 4th of July and so on and so forth, and then Pobrdzani, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Witness C, you mentioned, in your statement, that the old high-rise, Stari Soliter, where the fighting took place, was one of the key points from a military point of view as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you say the same for the high-rises of Poric and Novoteks, marked as number 2 and 3 on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I already said when high-rise 3 burned down in the second conflict on the 21st of October, 1992, from June onwards, it was used as a military stronghold of the BH army units, and the line went right by that high-rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what about high-rise 2, the Poric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: It's Poric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Poric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was never used by the members of the military because it was a civilian population that lived there, except for a few apartments that burned down also in October because they were hit by inflammable bullets from the old high-rise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right, you've already told us that. Mr. Usher, I believe that you can remove these documents now. I won't be needing them any more. Witness C, you mentioned today that religion was the personal affair of each and every soldier in the BH army and that they were enabled to practice their religion. Tell us, Witness C, since you worked in the sector for morale and information in the Territorial Defence staff and later in the BH army, as you said, did you ever have the opportunity of seeing a brochure which was published by the Mesihat of the Islamic community in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zenica in 1983 which is entitled, "Instructions to the Muslim Fighter"? I would ask the usher, please, to show D1 to the witness so that the witness could see whether he is familiar with this brochure or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I never had this kind of a brochure, and the distribution of this kind of a document did not go through the command of the unit that I was in, where I was assistant commander, and the general staff and the command of the 3rd Corps never issued any orders that would recommend or order this document to be used in the work of the organ that I worked in from '92 to '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've understood that. Do you know, Witness C, that this brochure was distributed to soldiers, not necessarily as you say, yourself, through the military structures but on a private basis through religious structures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I could not assess that, through which channels this kind of distribution might have taken place, I mean through religious structures, because I simply was never part of these structures so I do not know how they operated in other segments, including the one in which you are seeking an answer from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask you whether you personally have ever seen this brochure with any BH army soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it, but it is possible that they might have had it. Then maybe they received it through different channels, private channels or in villages, or in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, I won't be needing this exhibit any more, so could you please take it back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And now to conclude, Witness C, you said that in your official capacity first in the Territorial Defence and later in the BH army, you officially conducted a war diary, a logbook. Could you tell me the exact title of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Just as you said, the war diary. It is a big notebook, 100 pages, A-44 format, and it says, "War Diary, Hand-written".

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And in which language is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: On the front page, it didn't say so. I received orders orally in 1992 from the commander of the Territorial Defence, Mr. Refik Lendo, at the time this was kept, in terms of those matters that the municipal headquarters was supposed to deal with, and then from December, 1992, when I transferred to the brigade, then this was conducted for the 313th Brigade, Mountain Brigade of the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, do you recall when you handed over this war diary to the archives, what day that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I did not hand it over to the archives, myself. From the 308th Mountain Brigade, I went to the command of the garrison Travnik on the 26th of March, 1994, and it remained in the unit. And I assume that it was kept until the very end by the assistant commander in this area that I had operated in, too. That was my assumption, that it was kept as such until the Dayton Accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know where this document is today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know, but I know, from the period I spent working in the command of the garrison in 1996, that an order was issued for all documents from '92 to '95, according to the regulations on archives to be selected and to be handed over to the main staff of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness C. I have no further questions. Your Honours, I have thus concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Just a few clarifications. In respect of the date that was mentioned in the transcript, I want to be sure there was no mistake. Witness C, could you tell us the date when the 308th Mountain Brigade was created? The date was stated yesterday. I would like to be sure that the date is correct, that is, the date in the transcript says 7 December, '92, and I'd like to have your comment in respect of the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Lopez-Terres. I mentioned a few minutes ago that the 308th Brigade was established on the 17th of December, 1992, and that is the date of establishment of this brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So it's the 17th. Because in the transcript it said 7 December, not 17. Witness C, you were asked a few minutes ago, by Mario Cerkez's Defence counsel, whether you knew which units participated in the three conflicts about which you testified, and you answered, each time the question was asked, for the first, the second, and the third conflict, "I don't know which units they were." You stated, during your testimony here, that during the first conflict the forces who came from Busovaca and from Vitez had participated and you also said that in October, during the second conflict in October, '92, Busovaca forces had participated, and you also said that Kiseljak forces participated in that second conflict which lasted for a week; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but the attorney's question was whether I knew which units of the HVO took part. In response to that, I said I did not know the exact name of these units, but in my previous statement I said that there were HVO units or, rather, HVO forces outside Novi Travnik. We know this through the information that we received from the higher command and other information that I heard in headquarters from the commander of the staff, because when the June conflict took place, I was outside the headquarters and that is what I had stated previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So I can assume that when you say that you didn't know which units participated in the conflicts, you said that you don't know the names of the units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Names of the units. I said, by way of example, that I knew that the brigade in Novi Travnik was called Stjepan Tomasevic, but other names I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: That was the local Novi Travnik Brigade, but you confirmed that there were outside brigades which participated in the first and second conflicts in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Witness C. If you permit me, Your Honour, the first question had to do with the transcript. When I said there were two questions, in fact, I didn't include the first one which, in fact, from me, was a clerical error, and I would ask your indulgence for having expressed myself incorrectly when you asked how many questions I had to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly. That concludes your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have a second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This is the second question, it will be a very short one: This morning the question was asked about this declaration of war of April 1992, that is, the threat of the imminent danger of war and then the declaration of the war of 20 June, 1992. I would like you to tell us the following: When this threat of war was proclaimed on the 8th of April, 1992, the President of the Republic and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina invited all military-aged citizens to enrol with no distinction made between ethnic groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was a general proclamation that was applicable to the whole territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It never said it was addressed only to a particular ethnic group, or ethnic composition, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did many military-aged men of Croatian nationality present themselves as volunteers as well? Did they join the forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: I know that until the beginning of June 1992, at the registry office where people, that is, where military conscripts enrolled for the Territorial Defence, we had over 1.250 individuals, and that among them there were quite a number of people of both Croat and Serb ethnic origin who reported after this call was issued by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this was the possible list of conscripts, those who reported voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I want to ask you, what was the majority ethnic group that presented itself? Did Muslims enrol in larger numbers than did the Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C (resumed)
utterances.text: One did not try to analyse precisely this, the ethnic structure of those 1.250 volunteers, but the general impression when one goes through the names, one could say that Muslims -- people of Muslim ethnic origin or people of Bosniak ethnic origin were the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness C, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give evidence. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness, who will also be taken by Mr. Lopez-Terres requires no protection of any kind, so the court can be appropriately reconstituted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all right. It's the registrar I want to speak to. The name of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ismet Sahinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to sit down. Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Ismet Sahinovic, before we begin the testimony, I am asking you, out of respect for efficiency, to answer precisely but briefly and concisely. Answer my questions simply. If I need clarifications, I will let you know at the proper time. Mr. Ismet Sahinovic, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Forty-three. I was born in 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm the head of security at a plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what factory or what plant that is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: It is a factory manufacturing some military equipment and armaments and also has a civilian programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, did you live in Novi Travnik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Had you been living there for a long time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Between 16 and 18 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What was your position in the factory that you spoke about, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was a metalworker until 1991. In 1991, I was elected the Chairman of the union, and that was a professional position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As a factory worker and also as a resident there, were you associated in the meetings that had been organised within the business during which the company's business was discussed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You had access to all or most of the information about the company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, could you tell us whether you were a member or had been a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Social Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the functions that you occupied in the Bratstvo factory in Novi Travnik, and as the president of the workers' union, in 1992 how long did you carry out those responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Until about February or April -- February, March. That was about the time that I resigned and left the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the following period did you join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When exactly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Right after I left the position of the president of the union, and after I left the factory I offered my services to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict in the Novi Travnik municipality, between 1992 and '94, that is the conflicts that we're speaking about today, were you a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your responsibilities and your rank were within that army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, after I joined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I had no rank whatsoever. I was merely a soldier, a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities throughout that conflict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: When the battalion was formed, the second battalion within the Territorial Defence was formed, I was deputy commander responsible for morale in the battalion, until about November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And after 1992, November?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: After November '92, the commander of the municipal staff appointed me his deputy responsible for security matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were a soldier of the 308th Mountain Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you for those clarifications. Could you tell us, Mr. Sahinovic, whether during 1992 you had the occasion to meet the accused Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what those circumstances were?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, sometime in February, workers of the factory and I went out to a roadblock at a place called Okuka, which is the crossroads of Vitez to Travnik and Novi Travnik crossroad. We made that roadblock in order to draw the attention of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government, that it needed to solve our problems faster or, rather, the social status of the workers of the plant. Let me point out that before that, I went to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina twice and at that time I had talks with the then Prime Minister of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Jure Pelivan, and his deputy, Muhamed Cengic, and those talks were held towards the end of 1991, and they lasted until February '92, but the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not meet our requests, so that we had already announced previously, both to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the police, that we would block the road on the 24th February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the document Z2601, could you show us exactly where the roadblock that you're talking about was? I'm sorry, 2612A. 2612A.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, a suggestion. Is it possible to have the batch of maps that are going to be used either next to or not far from the witness so that we can speed up the time that we need to look for them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Which maps do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, we frequently present maps to the witness. First we have the -- can we have the maps that we used already? Can we have them near the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mean the maps given to, shown, or produce, rather, to the last witness; is that right? The maps of 2612, those maps, and, also, the maps of Novi Travnik. Are those the ones you want, 1962?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes. I was thinking of a general suggestion for this witness and for the future possibly, insofar as the maps have already been introduced. If we could have the maps next to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more convenient if they're kept by the registrar, otherwise, there is a danger of them being lost, but if before each witness gives evidence you tell us what documents or what maps you want him to have or her to have, no doubt we could accommodate that. Now, I think, for the moment, the maps of 1962 and 2612 should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the usher could take those and put them on the witness stand. It's not the big map, it's 2612. It's the photocopies showing the Travnik region. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, could you show us the location of the roadblock that you set up with the other workers from the Bratstvo factory, in 1992 in February, on the map?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the junction (indicating). The road coming from Vitez towards Travnik and here, to the left towards Novi Travnik (indicating). So I'm talking about this junction here (indicating). That was where we blocked the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You started to say this, but why did you set up the roadblock, set it up with the other factory workers? What was going on exactly in the factory at that point?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: For quite some time we had not received the salaries for our work, and we had large stocks in our halls. As far as I can remember, about $7 million worth of stocks we had. The programmes that we were doing then were done on the basis of a programme and contract with the Bosnia-Herzegovina government, and yet we were not allowed to send this to the end user, rather, to the client, the Yugoslav People's Army at the time. So we failed to persuade the government to intercede and protect the social status of workers, that we decided to block the road which was considered the main road. We thought that if we blocked the traffic, that we would be able to draw the attention of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government. We were intending to keep the road under blockade until somebody from the Bosnia-Herzegovina government came and did something to solve the problems, that is, met the requests that we had submitted to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Exactly what was going on at that point? What were they supplying?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: These were the armaments and materiel which was manufactured by the factory at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the roadblock that you set up, was it set up only by the -- was it constituted only by civilian vehicles and factory workers?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were the factory workers armed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the merchandise, you said that the merchandise that was stocked in that factory were the value of over several million dollars. You said that, "We were prevented from delivering it to the JNA." Who was the one that prevented you from delivering it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever a particular contingent would be ready, whenever we would load the trucks with this equipment, then -- and actually it happened in the village of Stojokovici and Bucici where the Croat population blocked the road because they would not allow that this equipment be delivered to the former Yugoslavia army, so that it also happened they would seize our trucks and the merchandise and to keep it, either keep an eye on it or just keep it for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How did the Croatian population of the village of Bucici, how did it hold the trucks back? How had it been informed that the trucks were going to go by?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of personally taking the trade from Novi Travnik to Busovaca, travelling with the security officer of the plant, and I then could see with my own eyes that there was no -- there were no roadblocks there. However, an hour later, when the convoy with armaments set off, this roadblock had already been put up by the Croat population in the village of Bucici. And two trucks came up, and a number of them were loaded with merchandise, but both those trucks were intercepted by the Croat population and were driven away to the village of Bucici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How long before the meeting with the accused Dario Kordic, about whom you're going to speak, how long had they been detoured?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Late '91, and those roadblocks were intensified, I mean the roadblocks impeding the delivery of equipment, military equipment, in early '92, and it reached Zenica, point of the culmination, in February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, it is now 11.15. Is that a convenient time to stop? We'll be getting on to the meeting with the accused; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres. You were coming to the meeting with Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, this is now the 24th of February, 1992, at that crossroads with the other factory workers. You set up a roadblock. You said that you met Dario Kordic at that crossroads. Could you give us some information, briefly, about the meeting and any conversations that you had with the accused at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: The strike committee that I had headed decided not to let any vehicles pass at that blockade except for ambulances and police vehicles. After the blockade, as far as I can remember, half an hour, an hour later, that was where we were, I mean at the crossroads, and a man came up to me and introduced himself as Dario Kordic. This person asked me, as chairman of this strike committee, that we let him pass the crossroads and go to Novi Travnik. However, since I did not know the gentleman in question until then, I decided that we would not let him pass, either, because after all, that was the attitude of the strike committee, too. This person told me that he was going to Novi Travnik precisely because of the problems and that the person in question would resolve these problems in Novi Travnik. However, I did not let him pass, and this person went away from me and I never saw this person again until the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the moments following Dario Kordic's departure, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, please? Please, sir. I didn't hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You've just said that you refused to let Dario Kordic pass through when he wanted to go to Novi Travnik. You said that he left and that you didn't see him again until the evening. What happened in the moments following the departure of the accused Dario Kordic? Now I'm talking about the roadblock, at that roadblock.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: After Mr. Dario Kordic left, persons in uniform started coming in. They were armed, so we had the impression that we were under control at that crossroads. These persons in uniform usually had masks, too, and you could only see their eyes. But in all fairness, there were some who had not been masked. I also noticed, on the right-hand side when you're going from Vitez to Travnik, we noticed from the houses there that there were some soldiers inside and that they were holding rifles at the windows of these houses. However, although these persons were armed, we decided to continue with the blockade of this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. What was the colour of the uniform that they were wearing in that area?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Black, and they had HOS insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of these HOS people that you're talking about, did you already know them? Had you had any dealings with them previously?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were the HOS people known in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, especially from the village of Bucici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What was their reputation in the region?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had black uniforms, and they made people afraid as soon as they would show up, especially when they were armed. And as such, they looked aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us about how many of those HOS members you saw around the roadblock and in the houses -- the house you're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: At the road, or rather at the crossroads where we were, I noticed 10 or 20 persons in uniform. However, I could not tell how many there were in the houses, because you could only see the barrels of their rifles sticking out of the houses that were on our right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did that group of armed men threaten you and the other people who had set up the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Soon after Mr. Dario Kordic left, another man came up to me, and he asked me whether I was the leader of the gang that was on the road. And he swore at me at that point. He cursed my balija mother. When I asked the person in question to tell me who he was, he introduced himself as Dario Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have a question. Could you give us the name of that person, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I thought I had heard you say "Dario". I had heard "Dario". So it's Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic. When I asked him what he wanted to talk about to me, he said that he did not want to talk to me, and he said, "You have five minutes' time to get this gang away from the crossroads. Otherwise, I'm going to blow all of this up." I was not afraid of these threats until I saw some men, most probably from his group, start tying explosives to the back of a bus, and then I realised how serious the threats were, the threats that were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The bus that you had put on the road is on the roadblock on the road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is the bus that we took when coming from the company and that we placed at the crossroads as a roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What happened after the explosives had been set up around the bus?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: When I realised how serious these threats were, then I used a loudspeaker that I had with me, and I told the workers to remain calm, to board the buses, and I said that they should go to Novi Travnik, to their homes. And as I came closer, I saw it was an interview he was -- Mr. Dario Kordic was giving for the radio/television of Sarajevo to a well-known journalist of the Sarajevo Television, Mr. Smiljko Sagolj. At that moment, I paused and I asked the general manager, who happened to be there, Mr. Jozo Krizanovic, "What's that supposed to mean, and what was that interview in front of the Bratstvo gate and what about?" But then the general manager simply patted me on the shoulder and said, "Don't you worry. He'll finish it and he'll be off." As I was talking with the general manager, I noticed -- rather I heard Mr. Dario Kordic speak about the historic moment for the Croat people and his personal commitment to prevent the delivery of materiel and military equipment and armaments from Bratstvo. I found it strange that a gentleman from Busovaca was giving an interview in Novi Travnik. And when the general manager urged me, I just went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, may we know when this interview took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I thought that I would ask that question once we had spoken about the -- actually seen the interview, because we have part of it in our exhibits. We're going to show a short part of that interview, the interview of Dario Kordic. I have asked that the text of the interview also be translated, and at this time we'll have the translation in both of the Tribunal's official languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Lopez-Terres, did what we see -- was it a television interview, is it part of a television interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, apparently it was an interview who was given to journalist, Smiljko Sagolj, who was from Sarajevo Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I arise again. We have never seen this, we have not been supplied with it. I don't know how long the Prosecution has had this particular tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The tape has not been disclosed to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The explanation for that is that it could not be formally established that the interview that we had was the one that the witness was talking about, that there was very little time. He has just arrived in The Hague, and the video cassette might not have been presented to us before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, again, it is much better if these matters can be disclosed before the witness comes to give evidence, because if they are not, it's possible that there can be delays. I'm not going to hold things up at the moment. Mr. Stein, we'll hear and see the video. If you've got an objection at the end of it, then, of course, you can make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, Sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number of this document is 53A and 53B for the translation, and the videotape is marked 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like to make it clear right away that after this first illustration, we also plan to distribute several -- rather to show some of a debate which was on television, in which the accused participated. These excerpts were translated, and the document which was translated has been given to you as part of the same document which was just given to you by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lopez-Terres, we must know the dates of these, the date of the interview and then the date of the debate. Can you let us know that now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I can't give you a specific date for the interview. The only thing that I can say, because I saw it, is that it was at a time when there was snow in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness can help us. Mr. Sahinovic, can you tell us when the interview took place?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I would not know the date exactly, but I'm quite positive that it was about a week or a fortnight after the events that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the debate, do we know the date for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The debate was more or less at the same time, because reference is made in it to the same discussion, by the fact that weapons had not been delivered to the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and the reporter who is interviewing the various participants, including Dario Kordic, is the same reporter who prepared the interview in front of the Bratstvo factory. If we could show the excerpt of the interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) "When we protested there, we also made it clear to the people who are in charge of this plant that should they continue what they are doing, they will be considered war criminals in the eyes of the Croatian people, and especially in the eyes of the people here who built this plant after the war, and that as such, they would have to account for themselves before these people. With this in mind, we and the people had opted for hunger, an option which is significantly different from receiving bloody, bloody -- blood-soaked dinars from Serbia which are in circulation in this area. Mr. Kordic --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Can we stop it for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, the short interview that we've just seen and which is the only one that we have, does it match what you talked about in respect of Dario Kordic and the factory that you spoke about as well?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. If I was accurate enough, when the gentleman talks about the historic moment for the Croat people and his efforts to stop the delivery of armaments for the Yugolav People's Army, and this interview that I can see now on my screen, this interview I never saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So it's another interview that the accused made?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in front of the main gate to the Bratstvo plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Let me ask the question a different way. The excerpt that you saw, it is not the part that you brought to us with the words of the accused, but can we say that this interview, in respect of where it took place, according to the position of Mr. Kordic, does it correspond to the one in which you partially participated in front of your factory?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So it's simply an excerpt of the interview which you did not participate in, yourself?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect, I appreciate the attempt to lay a foundation and tie what you've seen into the witness's testimony. I don't think it's, frankly, been done. But even if it has, it's apparent that this is part of a whole, and we don't have established on the record why this part was selected, if it's the only part selected. And to the extent that it's been edited, for whatever the reason and by whomever the editor is, it only shows part or a slice of the whole. Under the theory or the doctrine of completeness, I think it's in everyone's interests to see the entire interview, if it exists. If it doesn't, so be it, but we just don't know that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the absence of the entire video clearly goes towards the weight which is given to it. It doesn't prevent a clip, which this is, being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will, of course, bear in mind that it is only part and give it such weight as we think fit. Meanwhile, efforts should be made to find the whole tape. Mr. Lopez-Terres, no doubt some efforts can be made to find the rest of this tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I can tell you already that the part that was shown to you is the only part that the Office of the Prosecutor has. We don't have the entire interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, we accept that, and that's, no doubt, why you only played that part. What I'm saying is some effort should be made to find the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) As regards the second document, which I would like to present, for that we have the entire broadcast, but we made some selections because it's a broadcast that is longer than an hour, a televised interview that was prepared by the same journalist. We selected parts of it, excerpts that are going to be shown to you now, but it's been made clear that the Defence received the entire broadcast. The translation was given to you in both of the Tribunal's languages and in Serbo-Croat, only the parts that were said by Dario Kordic in the excerpts that were given to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we're going to see, what you're proposing to put in, is a debate on a day which is not known but was, you submit, shown on television, the witness not having seen it. Well, Mr. Stein, is the most sensible course not this, to play this tape now, or the excerpts which we have? You have the whole tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We do, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to play the whole tape, then perhaps you can find a convenient moment to do it, not necessarily during the examination of this witness, unless there's something relevant to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. If we could continue playing the rest of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could you stop it for a moment, please? We're not getting the English translation of what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've got the translation in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You don't need the interpretation? It was just a translation that I had, and that's why I've given it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't need the translation. We've got a transcript here. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) "Therefore, it had to establish a special status in this war, so that it would be considered with that status. With this in mind, we could not approve of the way that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina reacted to this problem up until a month ago, and we can say that to some extent we can be satisfied that in the last month it has begun more seriously to address the problem of the military industry, and has realised that this problem cannot be solved without the support of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, we do not accept that a proposal that exists only on paper that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina gives a guarantee, or rather allows certain possibilities to export these arms to other republics, that is to say, that there is no monopoly for the so-called Yugoslav army only, but that these arms can be exported to Croatia as well. Therefore, we have demanded that this be made possible in practical terms by sending some deliveries to the Croatian state and other, other entities, so that we could get a true insight into the veracity of those government decisions that were explicitly made. However, we had doubts, and the events of the last few days show that those are words on paper - a wish that hasn't become reality yet." "Q for KORDIC: Mr. Kordic, you have heard the general director, who said that it is the federal regulations still in effect in Bosnia and Herzegovina which are now blocking the factory." "KORDIC: Well, these federal regulations are obviously not binding on, let's say, Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, and if they are not binding on Bosnia and Herzegovina, then they are certainly not binding on the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, because the Croatian people cannot recognise these federal regulations which are null and void for us. So, we can only recognise the legitimacy of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but no federal regulations, no federal government, etc. I believe it is absurd to talk about this, about something that does not even exist."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Here is another excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) "This is not a secret, but the Croatian people were as armed as the Serb people, and these other two peoples had to pay for their armaments, so I think that it is not moral to put this kind of a question. I mean other peoples are being armed as well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The French interpretation has not been working now for about 10 minutes. I'm not getting any interpretation in French for the last five minutes or so. The last excerpts, I saw that -- I heard that it was working in English. I would like it to work in French as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm asking the interpreters in the French booth whether they have the translation in hard copy. All right. We were at the excerpt -- well, I think the translation stopped after excerpt 3. I think that the booth has the passage with, in the margin, the number "3", which indicates the passage in question. Would it be possible to show that excerpt number 3 again?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) "A question for Mr. Kordic from a viewer from Zenica. How can he decide about the people of Travnik and Busovaca? Let me say in response to your ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
