utterances.text: (Interpretation) Actually, that's not it. That's not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, help us with this. Where is the question in the French transcript? The question in the English transcript is on page 3 that you were referring to, the question to Kordic from a viewer from Zenica, "Who doesn't allow you to arm the people in Travnik and Busovaca." Now, where is that, please, in the French text?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The question -- rather at page 3 in the English document corresponds to page 4 in the French document, and Mr. Kordic's answer to that question about the Croatian people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's play that passage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is not that question, says the interpreter. It is not audible enough for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, unless this is done properly, we're not going to admit it. Now, is there anything of significance in this interview which the Prosecution particularly rely on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The Office of the Prosecutor shows in various paragraphs that were numbered from 1 to 5, because it believed that those parts, in respect of Dario Kordic's words, might be of interest in respect of the acts that are being dealt with in these proceedings. I have the impression that there is a difference in the pages here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the only way forward is to go forward without translation. We will play the tape. We have the transcript in front of us. We will read it. Now, do the interpreters get that? We simply will play the tape. There is no need for any translation at all. At the end of the tape we'll go on with the evidence. Now, can we play the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This is excerpt 4. Now we're coming to the last excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems rather a short tape for quite a long transcript but, still, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I apologise. I had no control over the translation or, rather, the interpretation today or the documents that were translated previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, at that time did you see the broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise who the people around Dario Kordic were during that discussion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give us the names of these people?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: The head of the municipality of Novi Travnik, Jozo Sekic. The man who worked in the military industry factory before that and, also, his deputy or, rather, the deputy Prime Minister of Novi Travnik Salih Krnjic and, also, the President of the SDA in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In respect of the broadcast that you saw, is it directly related to the events which were taking place in your factory at the time, that is, the fact that your factory was unable to deliver the arms that it had produced to the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, could you tell us, in a few words, how the conflict was resolved, that is, the conflict in respect of delivery of weapons that your factory had manufactured? In a few words.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting that I attended when I received direct threats from the members of the HOS, I was more concerned about my own fate and the fate of my family, but one of the conclusions was that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina should resolve this problem in Novi Travnik, especially, as far as I can remember, that the two trucks that were in the village of Bucici be returned to the factory. They had weapons on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At the time we're speaking about, there were two truckloads of weapons which had been diverted in the village of Bucici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the weapons being transported in those trucks?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Since I resigned after that, I left the trade union and position of president. Soon after that, I left the factory and I placed myself at the disposal of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You told us that you joined the Territorial Defence in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The trucks had been diverted at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Between February 1992 and May 1992, as far as you know since you were still in the factory, were the trucks given back?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards there was a meeting. I heard about it from the director. This meeting was with the gentleman from the Yugoslav People's Army, with the representatives of the government, but I don't know about this because I did not attend the meeting. I don't know whether they were returned, if they were returned at all, and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, do you know whether the accused, Dario Kordic, either obtained, or for the HVO, artillery pieces that came from your factory?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this gentleman came to Bratstvo. The security and the members of the TO, the Territorial Defence at the time, would not allow Mr. Kordic to enter the premises of the factory. However, when I put myself at the disposal of the Territorial Defence in the period from April onwards, in May 1992 I saw for myself a quantity of weapons that passed through Opara and the local commune of Zagrlje where I was in the Territorial Defence. The convoy passed during the night, after midnight, and that is when I personally saw three trucks. They were covered with tarpaulins. There were rocket systems of 262 millimetres, and there was also one truck of Oganj weapons, which is a 128-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you see the three trucks yourself as they went by in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some photographs that were given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If the usher would accommodate us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have just spoken to us about two types of weapons, multiple-rocket launchers, if I've understood you correctly, which were transported in the three trucks. Could you tell us whether the weapons you're speaking about, the weapons that you saw, were being driven in the three trucks that day? Could they or do they correspond to the photographs that you're being shown?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Is it possible, Mr. Usher, to put on the ELMO those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you make some comments about the photographs to us in respect of the three trucks that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These two trucks that you can see now (indicating), we're talking about the rocket system KOL, 262-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Does that system have a specific name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: It was only called a KOL, K-O-L multiple-rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was there another name used for that type of weapon, perhaps in respect of the calibre of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is the KOL, K-O-L, and multiple-rocket launcher. Those are the two terms that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I think that you had used the word Orkan before.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Orkan is different. That's a different weapon. This is KOL, with 16 barrels, and the calibre of the barrels is 262 millimetres. The Oganj has 32 barrels. So there is considerable difference between those two weapons, and you can see it when you look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The three trucks that you saw passing in the village that you spoke about, did they correspond to this type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give us some details about the three trucks, the trucks that were -- and what each one was carrying?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Since these were trucks that passed by and that had a tarpaulin cover, and at that time that was the latest product of our factory, our most up-to-date piece, although it was covered by tarpaulin, we could notice the difference between these armaments, because the tarpaulin is smaller and the Orkan is shorter. On the other vehicle there was an Oganj and that was different. So I know these two different weapons very well, and I can distinguish one from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Even though the trucks had covers over them, you were able to know what they were and what they were transporting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were able to do that because you were a worker in the factory? Is that why?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So that everything is very clear, could you tell us -- I'll ask you the question once again: In respect of the three trucks, exactly which weapons were they transporting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Two trucks carried the Orkan with the 262 millimetres, and one vehicle was carrying Oganj with a 128-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. When you saw the trucks going by, were you able to see in what direction they were travelling?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: They were going towards Novi Vakuf (sic) via Pavlovica. Where they went after that, that I do not know, so I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How were you able to learn that the trucks had some type of connection with the accused, Dario Kordic? How did you know that the trucks had to do with the merchandise that had been given to or taken by Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were civilian police checkpoints in the village of Opara, so these goods that were being transported were identified at that checkpoint. I received information about this subsequently as well from the police, that is to say, that a convoy of Dario Kordic had passed by. However, I wish to emphasise that I did not see Dario Kordic in this convoy, and I only recognised these three trucks or, rather, the kind of weapon that was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, that might be a convenient moment. It's 1.00. How much longer do you think you're likely to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) About 40 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like to correct a name, Your Honours, just before we begin. The witness, in respect of the direction that the three trucks took, he spoke about Gornji Vakuf, and I think in the transcript it said "Novi Vakuf", whereas it should be "Gornji Vakuf".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, that will be noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, I'm now going to give you a document which will be given to the Trial Chamber, and it is reference number Z78A. Let me make it clear that there are two documents that are covered by that reference number Z78, but that is the 78A and B. I am now asking for the Z78A. I would like the witness to review the document which has a seal on it. That is the Z78A. This is a document dated 22 April, 1992. Do you have the document in front of you, Mr. Sahinovic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, in the document is a description of three artillery pieces, two with 262 millimetre calibre and one 168 millimetres. Do the artillery pieces correspond to the heavy artillery pieces transported on the three trucks that you spoke to us about before the break?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: It's the same type of weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like you to pay attention to the document, Mr. Sahinovic. The upper part of the document has a title "BNT - TMIH" in the upper left-hand corner above the date. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what those letters refer to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know that, when it comes to this kind of delivery documents in the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'll ask you whether the "BNT" means anything to you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: "BNT" is the acronym for Bratstvo Novi Travnik company as a whole, and "BNT", which is Bratstvo, comprises also the hydraulic equipment factory which made armaments and ammunition. So, "BNT" means "Bratstvo Novi Travnik", a company which encompassed four or five different plants in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So we agree that the letters correspond to the letters of the Bratstvo factory?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the left-hand lower corner is a signature which has "Handed Over By". Are you familiar with the signature?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You never saw that signature?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, does the document correspond to the type of document that the Bratstvo factory would ordinarily draft at the time that we're speaking about, that is, April, 1992, where there were weapons or pieces of weapons that were to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the document, do you find any characteristics that would ordinarily appear in documents from the Bratstvo factory?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Bratstvo, or rather the machine hydraulics plant, when delivering armaments and military materiel, used a standard format of delivery documents. When I say "standard", then in the left corner there will be the name of the company in full, saying verbatim "Mechanical/Engineering Combined, Bratstvo" in the first line. And in the second one would be the mark of the specific plant, that is, factory of machinery and hydraulic equipment. Then in the third line there will be the date. In such documents, one always -- we always had the name of the person who made the invoice, the person who was delivering the merchandise, and the stamp of the plant. Here, however, I do not see the stamp of the plant, and I do not see the heading in the left corner. That is, I do not see that mark of the plant, so that I have never before seen such a delivery document in my factory before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the seal on the lower right-hand side of the document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, except for the name, that is, the first name and the last name that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was it customary for the Novi Travnik factory to include both the signature and the seal of the individual who was supposed to purchase or to take over the factory's materiel?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: On this invoice of the company, that is, the factory, for machines and hydraulic equipment, there was never the seal or the stamp of the receiving company or the end -- or the end destination, so to speak, receiving the merchandise, and this seal here, therefore, is very uncommon. It is not often seen on our documents, on the basis of which we deliver merchandise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like you now to review a second document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, before you go on, in the document Z78, in the English version, it refers, in the first line, to Ministry of the NO, National Defence, and further down we see the secretariat for the NO of the Busovaca municipality. And even further down, the Busovaca NO secretariat. Could the witness help us as to what "NO" means?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, could you answer the Judge's question, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, "NO", I believe, stands for "Narodna Obrina", National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Therefore, in the case in point, it would have to do with the secretary for defence for the municipality of Busovaca which is concerned by this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you have the seal of the secretariat for national defence of Busovaca. And as far as I can see, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would now like you to review a second document, Mr. Sahinovic. This is document dated 22 April as well and whose reference number is Z78B. This is a hand-written document also signed by the accused, the name of Dario Kordic, the difference being that there is no signature in the lower left corner. Have you already seen this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Would you look and see, as I do, that the document has exactly the same text as the text that you see in the typewritten document that we were speaking about just a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really read it properly because it is smudged, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, the copy is not very good.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: But the beginning of that text, I think, tallies with the typewritten text.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the middle part of the text --

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: -- there are references relating to artillery pieces. Are those the same artillery pieces as the ones in the document with the stamp of the Busovaca defence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is it the same -- are they the same armaments as those that were transported on the three trucks that you spoke to us about?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sahinovic. I would like to move to another subject now with Mr. Sahinovic. Mr. Sahinovic, during the conflict in Novi Travnik, did you lose one of your cousins?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give us that person's name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I lost my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: No, I'm speaking about your cousin.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the closest relative. My closest relative, my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you give us that cousin's name, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Muhamed Sahinovic, known as Cazo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, could you tell us under what circumstances your cousin died?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of June, the units of the Croatian Defence Council attacked the positions of the BH army in the area of Lazine. In that attack, the army of BH's line was broken through, and on that occasion my cousin was wounded lightly in the arm. He asked for help from the nurse, that is, the man who was taking the first-aid to companies, to a company also which was commanded by my cousin. After the first-aid was extended to him and both arms bandaged where he was wounded, he went back to the line not knowing that the line had been broken through, that is, that it had been taken by the units of the Croatian Defence Council. He was returning with the company's nurse, Hajder Mujic, and they were captured alive by members of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you were informed that your cousin had died?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was informed immediately, that day, when we learnt that the Lazine line had fallen and the Croatian Defence Council had taken over, the control over that line. We formed another defence line. We received information about fatalities, about missing, and captured. Among those captured was also my cousin and his nurse, rather, the company's nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Excuse me if this is difficult for you to speak about, but could you tell us whether you saw your cousin's body when it was given back?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you describe in what state that body was? Could you do that quickly, please, briefly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: It so happened that at that time, when the exchange took place or, rather, when the bodies of those two soldiers were driven over, I was a member of the Exchange Commission, so that I attended in person on that occasion, and I saw the bodies in what state they were. In that exchange from the Bosniak side, on behalf of the BH army, there was also present a doctor, Dr. Grizic, who then, in his capacity of a physician, noted that death occurred 24 hours before the exchange. The exchange took place in no-man's land, at a place called Trenica or Lager, to be more precise, and when we brought these bodies to Trenica, we then saw that the bodies had been massacred, both bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: We saw, and it was visible, that parts of the ears had been tied, that the genitals had been cut off, and even their eyes, I mean, had been gouged out, so that that body nobody could recognise except his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sahinovic. Do you have any information about the HVO forces who participated in the attack on the village of Lazine?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: According to information we had in the BH army, we heard that it was Novi Travnik units participating, supported by Vitezovi, that is Knights from Vitez, Knights unit from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What do you know about that Vitezovi unit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know much, except for a detail when a group of about 25 soldiers, armed, tried to enter from Vitez a Bosniak village which was on the boundary to Vitez, which was bordering on the mountain crest, and that is the boundary between Vitez and Novi Travnik, but all in that village were caught.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The Vitezovi were captured. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you yourself have the opportunity of speaking to members of that group?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you get any information about the group when the group was captured?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as some of these Vitezovi in the security service had been processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know who the head of the Vitezovi group was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know whether there is a connection between the people that you indicated as being HOS members and the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like to move to a final subject with you, Mr. Sahinovic, and this time this has to do with the second accused, Mario Cerkez. Mr. Sahinovic, did you have the opportunity, while you were a member of the BH army, to meet the accused Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can remember the date, but I will say that I met Mr. Mario Cerkez on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Tell us about the first time.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: The first time we met in Novi Travnik during the negotiations between the HVO, and the BH army, and the SDA, and the HDZ. As far as I know, Mario Cerkez was deputy commander in Novi Travnik, and that the commander was Boro Malbasic, was the commander, and he was also present at the negotiations. The date -- to the best of my recollection, it was in January, sometime around the 13th of January, 1993. The meeting was convened because the relations had deteriorated between the BH army and the HVO, particularly after units from Herzegovina, so-called Herzegovinians, arrived. They came on the 8th of January, '93. That is when they came to Novi Travnik. The arrival of those units and members of those units, I think the unit was called Bruno Busic, that unit that arrived in Novi Travnik. With their arrival, the expulsion of Muslims, Bosniaks gained momentum. The crime rate intensified and the torture of the remaining Bosniaks who had remained in the territory controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So the purpose of the meeting was to try to calm down the level of criminal activity; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did the accused, Mario Cerkez, participate in that meeting by taking the floor?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he did not take part in the discussion. The most active participant on the side of Croatian negotiators was the commander, Boro Malbasic, and the HDZ representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: At the time that you're speaking about, that is, January 1993, was Mario Cerkez stationed in Novi Travnik as a deputy commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What happened after the meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting that day, joint conclusions were agreed upon, and they were only supposed to be typed out and signed by the Bosniak and Croatian sides. However, at that meeting that was held in the main building of Bratstvo, we did not have the right conditions for doing so, so we were asked by the representatives of the Croatian side, Mr. Boro Malbasic, to go out for lunch to the lower part of town, specifically to the restaurant called Oskar, that lunch be prepared there and that we have lunch, and in the meantime, that the conclusions be typed out and that they be signed by both sides. However, I personally suggested to the Bosniak side not to go to HVO-held territory because of the problems that were intensified due to the arrival of the Herzegovinians. The Bosniak side did not listen to me, and they went to the restaurant called Oskar for lunch. Soon after that, during lunch, a group from Busovaca, a group of HVO members, surrounded the restaurant where this luncheon was taking place, and they took Bislim Zurapi, the commander of the brigade; and his driver; and Mevludin Berberovic, who was a member of the Bosniak group. They were put into a car and taken to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The commander that you're speaking about, was he the commander of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The 308th Mountain Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After how much time did Commander Zurapi go back or was he able to go back?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: They went in the afternoon. They went out for lunch and soon after that lunch they were taken away, that is to say, in the afternoon. It is only after midnight, at 3.00 a.m., that Zurapi was returned, because Refik Lendo intervened through Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you able to speak with Mr. Zurapi about what happened in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: He said that they didn't beat him then, they didn't mistreat him, except that they kept him, and once this intervention took place he was returned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: He never told us about the details. Mr. Bislim Zurapi never told us about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After the meeting which you say took place on the 13th of January, 1993, did you have the chance to see the accused, Mario Cerkez, again?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us when approximately and what was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say what the date was for sure, but I think it was about three or six months after this event. I met him in Vitez, at the HVO command in Vitez that was in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What was the purpose of your travelling to Vitez at that point?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: My superior officer gave me an assignment to go with the UN representatives, or rather the European Monitors, to go to Vitez, to the HVO headquarters with the commander of the HVO brigade from Gornji Vakuf and a member of the BH army from Gornji Vakuf. As far as I know, I was only needed to establish contact, Mr. Mario Cerkez and Hurim Nesad, who was commander of the battalion in Kruscica, and that contact was needed in order to exchange a Croat, whose name was Srecko, and a Bosniak from Kruscica. That was Senad Livnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The meeting took place at the Hotel Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was Mr. Blaskic there, there at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Exactly where was it that you met Mario Cerkez in the building called the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Upstairs. I cannot say exactly which room it was, but it was one of the offices. And then after that meeting, we went to the restaurant that was on the same floor. We went there to have lunch, and that is where we did have lunch after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember what Mario Cerkez said during that discussion that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was not familiar with all the details related to these two members of the HVO and the army and they were not from the municipality of Novi Travnik, it wasn't necessary for me to take part in the discussion at this meeting very much. But after the meeting, Mr. Cerkez said to me, "Give my regards to Commander Bislim and tell him not to send units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina via Skopjine Lokve. Otherwise, I'm going to kill them."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The name that you said corresponds to a place, does it not, because I'm referring back to the French interpretation. You gave a name. Could you tell us what that name corresponded to? I don't think that it was understood by the interpreters. Could you remind us of what it was that Mario Cerkez recommended at that moment when he spoke -- you said something about Skopjine. I don't --

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Skopjine Lokve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I saw "Skopljak" in the translation. I thought that was wrong. So, Mario Cerkez asked you to give his best greetings to Mr. Zurapi and recommended that you not send soldiers to that location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vitez, Kruscica, as far as I understood him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Not to send soldiers to Skopjine -- I don't remember the name, excuse me -- or to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not to send units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the 308th Mountain Brigade across the mountain of Skopjine Lokve to Vitez, to the zone of responsibility of Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you interpret those words as a threat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think the witness need answer that. It's a matter for us to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Let me summarise things here, because the translation is not really clear to me, at least as I see it. Mr. Cerkez simply said that, "We should not send soldiers to Vitez going through the Skopjine Lokve". That's the only thing he said; is that correct? He didn't make any other comments?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was that the last time that you met Mr. Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: The last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A final point I would like to take up with you, Mr. Sahinovic. While you were exercising your duties as a soldier in the 308th Mountain Brigade, did you meet any soldiers from the Croatian army near Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us on what occasion and at what time, if possible?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to define the time, but two or three times, for sure, I went to negotiate in the border areas of the municipality of Novi Travnik, Sebesic, Rostovo, because of the separation between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO. In '93, when the Herzegovinians left, I was on the commission with the members of the HVO for touring the front line. That is to say, both BH army lines and HVO lines that were supposed to be neutralised, and the trenches were supposed to be covered up. So these meetings of mine with the members of the HVO took place at least five times during the conflict between the BH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I asked you whether you had the opportunity to meet soldiers from the Croatian armies, and what I mean by that is the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question. Oh, so you're talking about members of the Croatian army. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yes, what is called in this Tribunal the HV.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us under what circumstances you met those members of the Croatian army from Croatia, the HV?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day, upon the arrival of the Herzegovinians in Novi Travnik, a group of Croatian policemen passed through Opara with a luxury passenger vehicle, and they were stopped at the checkpoint in Opara that was held by the military police of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As their IDs were scrutinised, that is to say, the IDs of the members of the Croatian army, it was nighttime and there wasn't enough light. The military policeman tried, through the open window of the car on the driver's side, to have a look at the IDs of the mentioned soldiers. However, the soldier who was the driver grabbed the member of the military police by the shoulders and dragged him into the car through the window. And when they got him into the car, then they escaped along the road to Novi Travnik. However, because of the speed involved, they were driving so fast, this same group skidded off the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Sahinovic. Mr. Lopez-Terres, do we need all these details?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'll ask the witness to summarise somewhat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You don't have to speak to us about the circumstances under which that person was arrested. The first question I would like to ask you is to know -- because you spoke about policemen and military. Were they members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How were you able to determine that they belonged to the military police from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrested them in Trenica, I personally interrogated the captured soldiers with a member of the police from Novi Travnik. Then judging by the IDs that they had on them, and those were badges of the military police of the Croatian Republic, and also the personal documents they had and that we had taken from them, all these documents and all the weapons that we had taken away from them, we took pictures of all of that, and thus we made documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How many people from the military police from Croatia were there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Three policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you interrogated those people, did they tell you what they were doing in the region?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: One of them was from Vitez. He was born in Vitez, and I think his name was Danijel Grebenar, as far as I can remember. He was the only one who was willing to talk about the circumstances under which they had come to Bosnia, and he personally confirmed that they came to train HVO soldiers in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I assume that you took those three men prisoner.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What happened to those three people subsequently? Were they released? And if they were, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: They were released on the second day. They were exchanged through the European Monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Exchanged for whom?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the Herzegovinians came in, two of our civilians were arrested and one soldier on the territory of the HVO in Novi Travnik, and they offered to have an exchange of these three persons whom they had arrested in Novi Travnik for these three soldiers belonging to the Croatian police. The next day, we did that through the European Monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly when you said three civilians had been kidnapped, arrested, so that they could be subsequently exchanged for the three Croatian military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I object to such question. There was a conclusion before the witness had the base for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree. Mr. Lopez-Terres, is there anything else now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is going to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, with all the other problems that we have already indicated to the Court, I do not want to repeat it, but today we have another problem, and that is the abundance of the material that was handed over to us. We do, however, understand the problem of time, so that we shall embark on our cross-examination immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sahinovic, I'm Mitko Naumovski, a lawyer from Zagreb, and I'm one of the Defence team for Dario Kordic, and I shall ask you a few questions. Perhaps we could begin part by part, but we might start from the event that happened on the 24th of February, 1992, when you organised the roadblock on the road -- or perhaps I should say the strike of Bratstvo workers. Tell us, please, when you decided to go on strike and when you took the decision to block the road, which was the body that took that decision?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the union had its union committee, and it coordinated all the activities between extraordinary workers, rallies, and all their activities, and the strike committee, which took -- and that committee took over the strike committee. It was the union committee as the highest union body in the plant. They became the strike committee, and it included Croats, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You're referring to the strike committee of the company?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Then you decided to block this principle road, as you showed us on the map, so as to draw the attention to your problems or the problems you had at the plant?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: It was because of the so-called status of workers, because their salaries were not being paid to them and because the Bosnia-Herzegovina government was very slow in solving our problems. We then decided to block that main road that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The then regulations, and I believe it is no different from other countries, but when a public rally is organised at a public place, then you need the authorisation of a relevant agency. At that time it was the police. You will agree with me? Will you please say it, because you can't nod your head.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You did not have the police authorisation to block the traffic at that place, did you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not the authorisation in writing, but we contacted the public security station in Novi Travnik and the public security centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We have to distinguish between two things. You do not have the authorisation to hold a public rally at a public place?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But neither did you have the authorisation to block the road, because that is the main thoroughfare. That is the main road in that area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not in writing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you decided to take law into your own hands at the moment when you decided to cut off the traffic and block the road, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: We then only were expressing the wish of the workers as manifested at the workers' rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you please answer my question? I said you took the law into your own hands, because without a written authorisation you cut, you blocked the main road.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We agreed that you had neither the authorisation for a public rally, let alone the authorisation to block the main road. The roads in the former state, in the former Yugoslavia and in the former Herzegovina, were not under the local police but a Ministry of Transport and Communications, and we've agreed that you had no authorisation to do that. It is precisely because of that that I'm asking, that is, I am inferring, rather, I'm affirming that at the moment when you cut into the main road, you took the law into your own hands. Very clear question.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So the fact that you interrupted the traffic on the main road, without any authorisation whatsoever, you do not think that that means taking the law into your own hands?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, because a month before that we had notified the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us do it step by step, please. Are you telling the court that you do not think that was an act of lawlessness?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not at all. If we notified the government and the Ministry of the Interior within the legally prescribed deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that. I'm not asking about whom you notified. I'm talking about authorisations.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood your testimony properly, that road was blocked until 1.00?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: For about 1.00. Within that hour, during that hour, that is the main road, there is always traffic, there must have been very many vehicles moving from both directions which stopped there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many, 100, 200 on the two sides?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say because I was at the crossroads, and I had the loudspeaker with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But there were vehicles on both sides of the crossroads. From how many directions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: From two directions, and the third one from Novi Travnik. So on the highway from two directions and also from the direction of Novi Travnik, which was the third direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So at this crossroads there were vehicles blocked from three directions?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I suppose people, that is, drivers or passengers, had got out of their vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I presume that those people gathered around the area where you were with that loudspeaker?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: More often than not they would come to the point where we gathered, and then they would usually go back to their vehicles, believing that it will be resolved quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but we can agree that for people who came and went, there were very many people because that was an event out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When Mr. Kordic came to you and introduced himself and gave you his name, he was wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: He did not have any military insignia or anything?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: He did not have any weapons, he was just a civilian?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You're saying that he told you, when he asked to be let through, that he was on his way to the plant to solve the problems?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not to the plant but to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Excuse me, Novi Travnik, but to solve the problems for which you had come out on the road?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And you still would not let him through?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please -- let us proceed with this: Some ten minutes after this detail, when Mr. Kordic asked you for permission, the soldiers that you described arrived?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Throughout the time that you were there, did you perhaps see Mr. Kordic with those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So that bit of the story that you are telling us has nothing to do with what happened later, I mean, this part with Mr. Kordic has nothing to do with what happened later?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see Mr. Kordic again until Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That's how I understood you. What happened subsequently had nothing to do with that detail which happened ten minutes earlier. You did not see that Mr. Kordic had anything to do with those men?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was clear. I did the not see Mr. Dario Kordic, after he approached me, until Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said HOS, H-O-S, would you please be so kind as to tell the court who were HOS members and what was it? What does that acronym stand for?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the acronym HOS stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You're right, but do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that in Novi Travnik, they were the first equipped and uniformed unit called HOS, H-O-S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: HOS, I believe, means Croatian armed forces. Have you ever heard that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But you've heard about the Croat Party of Right, which was active in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know that HOS was the military wing, if I may say so, of the Croat Party of Right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We can move on to that meeting that was held at the plant that day. What kind of a meeting was it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Not in the plant but in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. In the municipal hall. Who was present at the meeting. When the Prosecutor asked you, you gave a short answer, but could you be more precise? What kind of a meeting was that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: That meeting at the municipal hall in Novi Travnik, I do not recollect who convened it, but as far as I know, we waited at Okuka. That is the place where we made that roadblock. We were waiting for representatives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Were the government representatives coming to discuss the problems?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because as the manager had told me, they had learned about the newly arisen situation and let us know that they were on their way to Novi Travnik to try to solve those problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I did not hear that you told us. How many people were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: In the hall you mean? In the municipal hall, there were about 30 people present in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we could say there were quite a number of people present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The discussion was not quite peaceful in view of the Bratstvo problems and all that happened that day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was livelier than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Lively people were cutting in and everybody tried to present his views, in that sense, I mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I guess the views were opposed, weren't they? Naturally everyone was advocating his own point of view?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The management was speaking about legal regulations and provisions which they received from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the authority or permission to export them, but the gentlemen headed by Kordic were advocating, were upholding a different thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when you said that those soldiers came to that meeting, the HOS members, how did they address Mr. Kordic? What were the words they used when they addressed him?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was surprised when they addressed Mr. Kordic and did not address the head of the municipality, Sekic. They turned and addressed Mr. Kordic, "Why can't we attend it."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So they said, "Mr. Kordic"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Avdo Hebib, who came on behalf of the government to that meeting, was the Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But wasn't Deli Mustafic the Minister of the Interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was Hebib. Hebib was the Minister and it was in that capacity that he came to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, since we are talking about that event, perhaps we might also cast a look at that bulletin that was given to us today. In that bulletin, and I read it, as much as I could, and there are several theses here in this introductory part. It is this first long paragraph. Who wrote that paragraph and on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could the usher, please, with your leave, Your Honours, show the Croatian version, the original version of it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: The bulletin was written by the information service which existed within the Bratstvo system. That service published a weekly bulletin, and such bulletins were published as the need arose. I think it also says "Special edition."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It carries the date 26th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: There was one sentence which caught my eye, somewhere in the middle. Will you please look at it? It begins with the word "However." I think it is the third or fourth sentence in that first part, in the upper part. Third or fourth sentence it is. It begins with the word medjutim, "However." Have you found it? It's the fourth sentence from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: "However, as the political and security situation has changed in the country, this merchandise could not be delivered and this was explained by the local endeavours of the local political structures to allay or prevent the devastation and destruction at the fronts in the country."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: It says the word "country." What country is that? What country did they have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Presumably the person who wrote this would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But, Mr. Sahinovic, at that time you were the union leader, and you said you were a part of all that was going on at the plant, and you say this bulletin was yours, I mean, the latter part, the conclusions and the rest. So within that context, I think a very simple answer would be to say what devastation and destruction in the country. I mean, what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if you listen to me carefully, I said that I took part in the conclusions that were drawn at the union meeting, and the protest was sent to the Ministry of the Interior. The introductory part was written by the information service, and I believe I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The answer seemed pretty simple to me, but then I'm not going to insist on it any longer. Let us try to paint a picture of this period. This is February 1992 -- 1993. There was a war at the time on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, which started in 1991. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know that the attack on Vukovar took place after August 1991?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that in January 1992, Croatia was internationally recognised as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that at the time when this meeting was held, on the 24th of February, 1992, and when this bulletin was written two days later, the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia had left the Republic of Yugoslavia and proclaimed their independence? Will you please answer this?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do we agree with these facts, those I mentioned, that until this date, the date that we are discussing, the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatia had left the former Yugoslavia because they were proclaimed independent states?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's not controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you also agree with me that at this time, when this event occurred on the 24th of February, 1992, that Bosnia-Herzegovina had not decided on its fate?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I know that at that time Bosnia-Herzegovina had a census, had a government, and that we addressed that government as the only legitimate authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that at that time the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formally, legally, was within the remaining part of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know that the referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina took place after the date that we are discussing, the 24th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I know about the referendum but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The date was the 1st of March, 1992, after this.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I know. I know about the referendum but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do we agree then that it was only after the referendum or, rather, that at the referendum the wish was expressed, and in this particular case we're talking about Muslims and Croats, that Bosnia and Herzegovina become an independent state?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Not to tire the Honourable Trial Chamber with all this from this bulletin, let us perhaps draw their attention only to one thing. One of the requests that was put forth by the delegation or, rather, that was put forth by the Croats who attended this meeting was that weapons should not be delivered to the JNA, and that was the fundamental reason why they opposed the weapons leaving the factory. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you're telling the Honourable Chamber that the Croats did not insist on that, that the weapons should not be sent to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably know, those who were putting forth those requests then. I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But, Mr. Sahinovic, you were telling us about what had happened at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you tell us at least about one request that was put forth by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: They were categorical. They said they would not allow the weapons to leave the factory. I mean, for the former JNA. It was called the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps we didn't understand each other. That's just what I said. I'm asking you this because in this bulletin, on page 2, the bottom of page 2 of the version that you and I understand, you quoted the daily newspaper Oslobodjenje publishing an information about a government meeting which was held, that is to say, a day after this meeting on the 24th of February, that is to say, on the 25th of February, 1992, because the bulletin was printed a day after that, on the 26th of February, 1992, where it says that the government concluded inter alia -- obviously, this first part pertains to compensation for the workers in the factory, and it is said that they would compensate for the value of the production involved through goods that were in short supply, that is to say, meeting your social demands. And secondly that Bratstvo would independently contract with third persons things that belonged to the domain of their own production, and the SSNO -- and if we want to be understood better, that is the Ministry of Defence of the former Yugoslavia, they would not have a monopoly over it. That was basically the fundamental request that was put forth at this meeting that was held on the 24th of February at those talks; is that right? To simplify things, Mr. Sahinovic, so you will understand me, it is the buyer of the weapons that was contested, that is to say, the JNA, the military from the former Yugoslavia, as far as the present Croats are concerned?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps that is as far as the Croats got, but, no, our requests --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about your requests. I'm talking about the requests of the Croats who attended the meeting. I understand your requests.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. I talked about the requests of the Croats who attended this meeting, including Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I was quite clear. The gentlemen literally said that they would not allow delivery, although the director explained the decision of the government allowing the delivery to be completed from the contract from 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The delivery of weapons to who, to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. If I understood you correctly, after this period, that is to say, some two weeks later, please correct me if I'm wrong, this TV programme was broadcast, the one we saw today in the court with the journalist, Mr. Sagolj, Mr. Kordic and others having a discussion. This took place after this event; right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You know the video footage that the Prosecutor showed today, not the first introductory part but the one after that, you know, in the studio?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this detail from the studio. I only know about the interview in front of the Bratstvo gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you don't know when this other part was made?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity of seeing it before?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Now let us go back to the first part, if that is the only thing you know about that, that is to say, in front of the factory.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That part was not played to us, but you will agree with me that you said that Mr. Kordic then said to the journalist, Mr. Sagolj, I'm quoting, "As a representative of the Croatian people in Central Bosnia, he will never allow weapons to be delivered to the JNA." I think that that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that is not what I said. If you understood me correctly, I said Mr. Kordic at that point in time was telling Smiljko Sagolj, "This is a historical moment that I created for the Croatian people, that weapons from the factory of Bratstvo Novi Travnik cannot be delivered to the Yugoslav People's Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we agree on that, that that was said on the 24th of February, 1992, in front of the Bratstvo factory?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not on the 24th in front of the Bratstvo factory. I said that this was 15 or 20 days after the blockade of the road, as far as I can remember. It wasn't on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At the same place where the factory is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So if I have misunderstood me (sic), I apologise. I accept what you're saying. So this was said sometime in March; March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we agree that this was after the referendum that Bosnia and Herzegovina had and by which it proclaimed its independence, if the referendum took place on the 1st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I said that I did not know the date of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm saying that it was on the 1st of March, and you can check it, if you want. The Prosecutor played us a tape today, and we managed to understand the text. Perhaps the other people in the courtroom didn't. So could you please comment on two words I noted? We heard Mr. Kordic say the following: Could the usher please show Mr. Sahinovic 53B? It is 53B. It is the first section that the Prosecutor marked with the Roman Numeral I over here on page 1. You see the Roman Numeral I on the top up here?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This last sentence, we heard Mr. Kordic say, "If that is so, we and the people have opted for hunger, an option which is significantly different from receiving bloody, bloody dinars from Topcider," a printing press in Serbia, "soaked in blood which are in circulation in this area." I don't think that we should retell this and try to explain what Mr. Kordic meant. I just wanted you to tell the Honourable Court what this "dinars of Topcider" means. Do you know where money was printed in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I know it was in Belgrade, but I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In Topcider. You heard of Topcider?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So we will agree that these are Yugoslav dinars?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: These are Yugoslav dinars; right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, but in that situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish. It is not weapons that were important to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I understand your explanation, Mr. Sahinovic. You presented your point of view, and I think that you did so very accurately to the Honourable Judges and to all of us. But please answer my questions now. You agree with what I said, that these are Yugoslav dinars. Perhaps that will not be quite clear to the Honourable Judges from this, that is to say, Topcider, so do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So these are not Yugoslav dinars?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not agree with you, because at that time that was the only way that we, the workers -- I mean that was the only money that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. So then I'm going to put it this way: Who did you, the workers, insist on getting money from for the goods that you manufactured?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: From the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Not for those for whom you made these weapons, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SAHINOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to seek your assistance, so to speak. Today, a videotape was presented from a TV programme in which Mr. Mario (sic) Kordic took part, in addition to the journalist, and also the president of the SDP from Novi Travnik, Salih Krnjic, and also the head of the municipality, Jozo Sekic. The witness who was present here today says that this is the first time he ever saw it, that today is the first time he ever saw it. But since this video was played before you today, I have no other choice but to use those few parts that the Prosecutor used and to put a few questions in relation to that, or rather to draw your attention to a few sentences from there. That is what the Prosecutor did today. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, there's very little point putting it to the witness if he didn't see the programme. But, of course, if you've got some comments that you want to make about it, then you can do that. It may be after the witness has given his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour. That is why I sought your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now just after 4.00. Do you have very much more?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid I do need more time. I cannot finish by quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sahinovic, we're adjourning now. Could you be back, please, tomorrow morning at 9.45 to conclude your evidence? Would you remember, in this adjournment and in any others there may be, not to speak to anybody about your evidence and not to let anybody speak to you about it? And that includes members of the Prosecution team, who, since you have started giving evidence, are not allowed to speak to you during the course of your evidence. So don't speak to anybody about it, please. And would you be back at 9.45? Mr. Nice, is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A tiny point, and I can deal with it in the presence of the witness unless -- I think I probably can. Mr. Lopez-Terres is due elsewhere tomorrow. I hope it will be acceptable if I deal with any necessary re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.03 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of April, 1999, at 9.45 a.m.
